course.title: AP U.S. History
course.description: Trace how Americans have argued over identity, power, work, and their place in the world, from the societies that existed before 1491 to the present.
course.previewDescription: Follow the nation's development from early contact and colonization through independence, civil war, industrialization, world wars, and recent decades.

unit.title: Period 4
unit.description: Follow the rise of party politics and a more participatory democracy, the market revolution, westward expansion and foreign policy, the Second Great Awakening and reform, and the growth of slavery from 1800 to 1848.

framework.name: Course themes
framework.title: Use the course themes to choose your evidence
framework.intro: The themes connect developments across all nine periods. A piece of evidence can fit more than one theme; choose the one that answers the prompt.
framework.sourceNote: Theme names, codes, and descriptions follow the AP U.S. History Course and Exam Description (fall 2026).

themes.title: American and National Identity
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why definitions of American and national identity and values have developed among the diverse and changing population of North America as well as on related topics, such as citizenship, constitutionalism, foreign policy, assimilation, and American exceptionalism.
themes.question: Who counted as American, and what did people believe the nation stood for?
themes.example: Debates over ratifying the Constitution turned on what kind of republic Americans wanted.

themes.title: Work, Exchange, and Technology
themes.description: This theme focuses on the factors behind the development of systems of economic exchange, particularly the role of technology, economic markets, and government.
themes.question: How did people earn a living, trade, and use new technology?
themes.example: Canals and railroads tied farmers in the West to markets in the East.

themes.title: Geography and the Environment
themes.description: This theme focuses on the role of geography and both the natural and human-made environments in the social and political developments in what would become the United States.
themes.question: How did land, climate, and resources shape choices, and how did people change them?
themes.example: The Chesapeake's climate suited tobacco, which shaped its labor system.

themes.title: Migration and Settlement
themes.description: This theme focuses on why and how the various people who moved to and within the United States both adapted to and transformed their new social and physical environments.
themes.question: Why did people move, and how did they change the places they settled?
themes.example: The Great Migration brought African Americans from the rural South to northern cities.

themes.title: Politics and Power
themes.description: This theme focuses on how different social and political groups have influenced society and government in the United States as well as how political beliefs and institutions have changed over time.
themes.question: Who held power, how did they use it, and who challenged it?
themes.example: The New Deal expanded the federal government's role in the economy.

themes.title: America in the World
themes.description: This theme focuses on the interactions between nations that affected North American history in the colonial period and on the influence of the United States on world affairs.
themes.question: How did contact, trade, diplomacy, and war connect America to other nations?
themes.example: The Seven Years' War left Britain in debt and changed its policies toward the colonies.

themes.title: American and Regional Culture
themes.description: This theme focuses on the how and why national, regional, and group cultures developed and changed as well as how culture has shaped government policy and the economy.
themes.question: How did beliefs, religion, arts, and media develop and shape public life?
themes.example: The Second Great Awakening inspired many Americans to join reform movements.

themes.title: Social Structures
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why systems of social organization develop and change as well as the impact that these systems have on the broader society.
themes.question: How were people ranked by race, class, and gender, and how did that change?
themes.example: The growth of a middle class in the Gilded Age changed ideas about leisure and family.

lesson.title: America on the World Stage
lesson.summary: How the War of 1812, border agreements with Britain and Spain, and the Monroe Doctrine expressed a growing American effort to claim territory, protect trade, and assert influence in the Western Hemisphere.
learningGoals: Explain the causes and effects of the War of 1812.
Explain how treaties and agreements fixed U.S. borders in North America.
Explain the purposes and significance of the Monroe Doctrine.
lesson.bigIdea: The United States tried to create an independent global presence by claiming territory across the continent, defending its trade, and warning European powers away from the Western Hemisphere.
lesson.context: The CED asks you to explain how and why American foreign policy developed and expanded. Pair each action with its aim: security, trade, or territory.

sections.title: The War of 1812

blocks.text: Struggling to create an independent global presence, the United States sought to claim territory throughout the North American continent and promote foreign trade. Britain and France continued to interfere with American shipping in their wars, and Britain impressed sailors from American ships, which angered many Americans. In the West, settlers blamed the British for supporting Native resistance. The Shawnee leader Tecumseh and his brother Tenskwatawa built a confederacy of Native nations to resist the loss of land, and U.S. forces under William Henry Harrison defeated them at Tippecanoe in 1811.

A group of young congressmen from the South and West, called War Hawks, pushed for war, and Congress declared war on Britain in June 1812. The fighting included the British burning of Washington in 1814, the defense of Baltimore that inspired the “Star-Spangled Banner,” and Andrew Jackson's victory at New Orleans in January 1815, which took place after the peace treaty had been signed at Ghent in December 1814. The treaty restored the situation before the war.

The war's effects were large even though it ended without territorial change. It strengthened national feeling, weakened the Federalist Party after its Hartford Convention criticized the war, destroyed Tecumseh's confederacy and weakened Native resistance east of the Mississippi, and encouraged American manufacturing by cutting off British imports.

sections.takeaway: The war grew out of conflicts over trade and the frontier, and it ended in a draw that strengthened national feeling and weakened Native resistance.

sections.title: Diplomacy and borders

blocks.text: After the war the United States settled its borders through diplomacy. The Rush–Bagot Agreement of 1817 limited naval forces on the Great Lakes, and the Convention of 1818 set the northern boundary between the Louisiana Purchase and British Canada at the 49th parallel and provided for joint American and British occupation of the Oregon Country.

In the Adams–Onís Treaty of 1819, Spain gave Florida to the United States and accepted a boundary that ran to the Pacific, which gave the United States a claim on the Pacific coast. These agreements reduced the British and Spanish presence on the nation's borders without war.

sections.takeaway: Treaties with Britain and Spain fixed the northern boundary, gave the United States Florida, and extended its claims to the Pacific.

sections.title: The Monroe Doctrine

blocks.text: The U.S. government sought influence and control over the Western Hemisphere through a variety of means, including military actions, American Indian removal, and diplomatic efforts such as the Monroe Doctrine. In the 1810s and 1820s, most of Spain's colonies in Latin America won independence, and European monarchies talked of helping Spain regain them. Britain, which wanted to keep trade with the new nations, proposed a joint statement, but Secretary of State John Quincy Adams urged the United States to act on its own.

In his annual message of December 1823, President James Monroe declared that the United States would regard any attempt by a European power to extend its system to any part of the Western Hemisphere as dangerous to the nation's peace and safety. He also said that the United States would not interfere with existing European colonies and would not take part in European wars. The Monroe Doctrine had little force at the time, because the United States lacked the strength to enforce it, and British naval power protected the new nations. Later presidents invoked it to justify American influence in the hemisphere.

blocks.title: Common trap
blocks.text: The Monroe Doctrine was a statement of policy and not a treaty or an alliance. In 1823 it was effective mainly because Britain's navy also opposed European intervention.

sections.takeaway: The Monroe Doctrine warned Europe against intervening in the Western Hemisphere, and it later became a foundation of American foreign policy.

connections.title: The economy behind the foreign policy
connections.body: The wish for trade and territory had a domestic side. Topic 4.5 follows the transformation of production and transportation.
connections.transferQuestion: How did the War of 1812 contribute to the growth of American manufacturing?
connections.feedback: A strong answer notes that the war and the earlier embargo cut off British imports, which encouraged Americans to invest in domestic factories.
